Read About Sharm El Sheikh

A resort city best understood through its reef-lined coast, desert edge and distinct bays.

THE RED SEA SETS THE RHYTHM

Sharm El Sheikh sits at Sinai’s southern tip, where hotel districts face clear Red Sea water and the mountains begin just beyond the built-up coast. Naama Bay is the easy first orientation: a recognisable waterfront with dining, beach time and evening movement. North of it, SOHO Square and Shark’s Bay make a separate airport-side cluster.

The strongest days keep land and water in balance: reef time early, then a slow evening on shore.

THE PARK IS THE COUNTERPOINT

Ras Muhammad National Park is the guide’s full-day nature anchor. Its desert headlands, mangrove habitat and snorkeling sites make it more than a beach transfer. Conditions matter here: follow the operator and park briefing, and treat the water plan as weather-dependent rather than fixed.

BEYOND THE RESORT STRIP

The Old Market and the Al Sahaba Mosque offer a denser city-facing contrast to the resort frontage. They work best toward late afternoon, when browsing, a café stop and the mosque’s silhouette can share one unhurried outing.
